title: Finite-Dimensional Vector Spaces and Dimension
---

The notion of *dimension* will appear constantly throughout linear algebra and beyond. Finite-dimensional vector spaces are determined up to isomorphism by a single integer, their dimension. We establish this through a sequence of lemmas about the interplay between spanning lists and linearly independent lists.

:::definition{4.7.1} Finite-dimensional
A vector space $V$ is ***finite-dimensional*** if it has a finite spanning list, i.e., vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ with $\Span(v_1, \ldots, v_n) = V$. Otherwise, $V$ is ***infinite-dimensional***.
:::

## <span class="num">4.7.1</span> Extracting Bases from Spanning Lists

Our first result shows that every finite spanning list contains a basis.

:::lemma{4.7.2} Spanning lists contain bases
If $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ span $V$, then some sublist of $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is a basis of $V$.
:::

:::proof
We construct a basis by removing redundant vectors one at a time.

If $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ are linearly independent, they already form a basis. Otherwise, there is a nontrivial relation $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i = 0$ with some $a_j \neq 0$. Then $$v_j = -\frac{1}{a_j} \sum_{i \neq j} a_i v_i \in \Span(v_i : i \neq j).$$ So the list with $v_j$ removed still spans $V$: in any linear combination of $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ we can substitute this expression for $v_j$.

Remove $v_j$ and repeat. Since the list is finite, the process terminates, and when it does, the remaining vectors are linearly independent and still span $V$, so they form a basis. (If $V = \{0\}$, we may end with the empty list, which is a basis of $\{0\}$.)
:::

:::corollary{4.7.3} Finite-dimensional spaces have bases
Every finite-dimensional vector space has a finite basis.
:::

## <span class="num">4.7.2</span> Extending Linearly Independent Lists to Bases

The dual result shows that every linearly independent list can be enlarged to a basis.

:::lemma{4.7.4} Linearly independent lists extend to bases
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional and let $v_1, \ldots, v_m \in V$ be linearly independent. Then $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ can be extended to a basis of $V$. More precisely, if $w_1, \ldots, w_r$ span $V$, then appending suitable vectors among $w_1, \ldots, w_r$ to $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ gives a basis of $V$.
:::

:::proof
Let $w_1, \ldots, w_r$ span $V$; such a list exists because $V$ is finite-dimensional. For $j = 0, 1, \ldots, r$ let $$W_j = \Span(v_1, \ldots, v_m, w_1, \ldots, w_j).$$ We show by induction on $j$ that $W_j$ has a basis consisting of $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ followed by some of $w_1, \ldots, w_j$. For $j = 0$, the list $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ is independent and spans $W_0$, so it is a basis.

Suppose $\mathcal{B}_{j-1}$ is such a basis of $W_{j-1}$. If $w_j \in W_{j-1}$, then $W_j = W_{j-1}$ and we keep $\mathcal{B}_j = \mathcal{B}_{j-1}$. If $w_j \notin W_{j-1} = \Span(\mathcal{B}_{j-1})$, then $\mathcal{B}_j = (\mathcal{B}_{j-1}, w_j)$ is linearly independent by Lemma [4.6.6](/notes/math-55a/4-6-span-linear-independence-and-bases#lemma-4-6-6), and it spans $W_j$, since $\Span(\mathcal{B}_j)$ contains $W_{j-1}$ and $w_j$. Either way $\mathcal{B}_j$ is a basis of $W_j$ of the required form.

Finally, $W_r \supseteq \Span(w_1, \ldots, w_r) = V$, so $\mathcal{B}_r$ is a basis of $V$ containing $v_1, \ldots, v_m$.
:::

## <span class="num">4.7.3</span> The Exchange Lemma and Invariance of Dimension

The next lemma is the heart of the theory: it compares the lengths of independent lists and spanning lists. Its proof exchanges vectors of a spanning list, one at a time, for vectors of an independent list.

:::lemma{4.7.5} Exchange lemma
If $u_1, \ldots, u_m$ are linearly independent in $V$ and $w_1, \ldots, w_n$ span $V$, then $m \leq n$.
:::

:::proof
We show by induction on $j = 0, 1, \ldots, m$ that $j \leq n$ and that, after renumbering the $w$’s, the list $$u_1, \ldots, u_j, w_{j+1}, \ldots, w_n$$ spans $V$. For $j = 0$ this is the hypothesis. Suppose it holds for some $j < m$. Since the list spans $V$, we can write $$u_{j+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{j} b_i u_i + \sum_{l=j+1}^{n} c_l w_l.$$ If all the $c_l$ were zero (in particular, if $j = n$ and no $w$’s are left), then $u_{j+1}$ would be a linear combination of $u_1, \ldots, u_j$, contradicting the independence of the $u$’s. So $j + 1 \leq n$, and after renumbering we may assume $c_{j+1} \neq 0$. Solving for $w_{j+1}$, $$w_{j+1} = c_{j+1}^{-1}\Big(u_{j+1} - \sum_{i=1}^{j} b_i u_i - \sum_{l=j+2}^{n} c_l w_l\Big) \in \Span(u_1, \ldots, u_{j+1}, w_{j+2}, \ldots, w_n).$$ So this span contains $u_1, \ldots, u_j, w_{j+1}, \ldots, w_n$, which span $V$; hence it is $V$. This completes the induction, and the case $j = m$ gives $m \leq n$.
:::

:::theorem{4.7.6} All bases have the same size
If $V$ has a basis with $n$ elements, then every basis of $V$ has exactly $n$ elements.
:::

:::proof
Let $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ be a basis and $\mathcal{B}'$ another basis of $V$. Any $m$ distinct elements of $\mathcal{B}'$ are linearly independent, and $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ span $V$, so $m \leq n$ by the exchange lemma. Hence $\mathcal{B}'$ is finite, with $m \leq n$ elements. Exchanging the roles of the two bases gives $n \leq m$.
:::

:::definition{4.7.7} Dimension
The ***dimension*** of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, denoted $\dim V$ or $\dim_k V$, is the number of elements of any basis of $V$. By the theorem this does not depend on the basis. The empty set is a basis of the zero space, so $\dim \{0\} = 0$. If $V$ is infinite-dimensional we write $\dim V = \infty$.
:::

:::corollary{4.7.8} Independent and spanning lists in dimension $n$
Let $\dim V = n$.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. Every linearly independent list in $V$ has at most $n$ vectors, and every spanning list has at least $n$ vectors.
2. A linearly independent list of $n$ vectors is a basis, and so is a spanning list of $n$ vectors.
:::

:::proof
(a) Apply the exchange lemma with a basis of $V$ as the spanning list, respectively as the independent list.

(b) By Lemma [4.7.4](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#lemma-4-7-4), an independent list of $n$ vectors extends to a basis, which has $n$ elements, so no vectors were added. By Lemma [4.7.2](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#lemma-4-7-2), a spanning list of $n$ vectors contains a basis, which has $n$ elements, so no vectors were removed.
:::

:::corollary{4.7.9} Classification of finite-dimensional spaces
Every vector space $V$ of dimension $n$ is isomorphic to $k^n$. Two finite-dimensional vector spaces are isomorphic if and only if they have the same dimension.
:::

:::proof
Let $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ be a basis of $V$. The map $$\Phi : k^n \to V, \quad (a_1, \ldots, a_n) \mapsto \sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i$$ is linear, injective by Proposition [4.6.5](/notes/math-55a/4-6-span-linear-independence-and-bases#proposition-4-6-5) and surjective because the $v_i$ span; so it is an isomorphism.

If $\varphi : V \to W$ is an isomorphism and $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is a basis of $V$, then $\varphi(v_1), \ldots, \varphi(v_n)$ is a basis of $W$. It spans, since every $w \in W$ is $\varphi(v)$ for some $v = \sum a_i v_i$, so $w = \sum a_i \varphi(v_i)$. It is independent, since $\sum a_i \varphi(v_i) = 0$ means $\varphi(\sum a_i v_i) = 0 = \varphi(0)$, so $\sum a_i v_i = 0$ by injectivity and all $a_i = 0$. Hence isomorphic spaces have the same dimension. Conversely, two spaces of dimension $n$ are both isomorphic to $k^n$, hence to each other.
:::

:::note
The isomorphism $\Phi : k^n \xrightarrow{\sim} V$ depends on the *choice of basis*, and different bases give different isomorphisms. Choosing a basis amounts to choosing coordinates: we represent $v = \sum a_i v_i$ by the ***column vector*** $\begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ \vdots \\ a_n \end{pmatrix} \in k^n$ of its coordinates. Much of linear algebra consists in using coordinates when they help and avoiding them when they do not.
:::

## <span class="num">4.7.4</span> Subspaces of Finite-Dimensional Spaces

:::proposition{4.7.10} Subspaces of finite-dimensional spaces
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional and $U \subseteq V$ a subspace. Then $U$ is finite-dimensional and $\dim U \leq \dim V$, with equality if and only if $U = V$.
:::

:::proof
Let $n = \dim V$. By the exchange lemma, every linearly independent list in $U$ has at most $n$ vectors, since it is also independent in $V$. Choose an independent list $u_1, \ldots, u_m$ in $U$ of the largest possible length; then $m \leq n$. It spans $U$: if some $u \in U$ were not in $\Span(u_1, \ldots, u_m)$, then $u_1, \ldots, u_m, u$ would be a longer independent list in $U$ by Lemma [4.6.6](/notes/math-55a/4-6-span-linear-independence-and-bases#lemma-4-6-6). So $u_1, \ldots, u_m$ is a basis of $U$, and $\dim U = m \leq n$.

If $U = V$, the dimensions agree. If $\dim U = n$, a basis of $U$ is a linearly independent list of $n$ vectors in $V$, hence a basis of $V$ by Corollary [4.7.8](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#corollary-4-7-8); so $V = \Span(u_1, \ldots, u_n) \subseteq U$, and $U = V$.
:::

:::proposition{4.7.11} Complements exist
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional and $U \subseteq V$ a subspace. Then there is a subspace $W \subseteq V$ with $V = U \oplus W$.
:::

:::proof
By Proposition [4.7.10](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#proposition-4-7-10), $U$ has a basis $u_1, \ldots, u_m$. Extend it to a basis $u_1, \ldots, u_m, w_1, \ldots, w_s$ of $V$ (Lemma [4.7.4](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#lemma-4-7-4)) and let $W = \Span(w_1, \ldots, w_s)$. Every $v \in V$ is a linear combination of the $u_i$ and $w_j$, so $V = U + W$. If $v \in U \cap W$, then $v = \sum a_i u_i = \sum b_j w_j$, so $\sum a_i u_i - \sum b_j w_j = 0$, and independence gives $a_i = b_j = 0$; thus $v = 0$.
:::

A subspace $W$ with $V = U \oplus W$ is called a ***complement*** of $U$ in $V$. It is far from unique: in $k^2$, every line through the origin other than $U = \{(a, 0)\}$ is a complement of $U$.

## <span class="num">4.7.5</span> Dimension of Sums and Direct Sums

:::theorem{4.7.12} Dimension formula for sums
Let $U$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space $V$. Then $U + W$ is finite-dimensional and $$\dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W).$$ In particular, if the sum is direct, then $\dim(U \oplus W) = \dim U + \dim W$.
:::

:::proof
The subspace $U \cap W$ of $U$ is finite-dimensional by Proposition [4.7.10](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#proposition-4-7-10). Let $v_1, \ldots, v_r$ be a basis of $U \cap W$. By Lemma [4.7.4](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#lemma-4-7-4), extend it to a basis $v_1, \ldots, v_r, u_1, \ldots, u_m$ of $U$ and to a basis $v_1, \ldots, v_r, w_1, \ldots, w_n$ of $W$. We claim that $$v_1, \ldots, v_r, u_1, \ldots, u_m, w_1, \ldots, w_n$$ is a basis of $U + W$.

*Spanning:* Any $x \in U + W$ is $x = u + w$ with $u \in U$ and $w \in W$. Writing $u$ and $w$ in the bases above expresses $x$ as a linear combination of the listed vectors.

*Independence:* Suppose $\sum a_i v_i + \sum b_j u_j + \sum c_l w_l = 0$. Then $$\sum c_l w_l = -\sum a_i v_i - \sum b_j u_j \in U.$$ Since also $\sum c_l w_l \in W$, it lies in $U \cap W$, so $\sum c_l w_l = \sum d_i v_i$ for some scalars $d_i$. Then $\sum d_i v_i - \sum c_l w_l = 0$, and since $v_1, \ldots, v_r, w_1, \ldots, w_n$ is a basis of $W$, all $c_l = 0$. Now $\sum a_i v_i + \sum b_j u_j = 0$, and since $v_1, \ldots, v_r, u_1, \ldots, u_m$ is a basis of $U$, all $a_i$ and $b_j$ vanish.

Thus $\dim(U + W) = r + m + n = (r + m) + (r + n) - r = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W)$.
:::

:::corollary{4.7.13} Recognizing a direct sum decomposition
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional and $U, W \subseteq V$ subspaces. Then $V = U \oplus W$ if and only if $U \cap W = \{0\}$ and $\dim U + \dim W = \dim V$.
:::

:::proof
If $V = U \oplus W$, then $U \cap W = \{0\}$ and the formula gives $\dim V = \dim U + \dim W$. Conversely, under the two conditions the formula gives $\dim(U + W) = \dim V$, so $U + W = V$ by Proposition [4.7.10](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#proposition-4-7-10).
:::

:::proposition{4.7.14} Dimension of a direct sum
<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. If $V = U_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus U_n$ and each $U_i$ is finite-dimensional, then putting together bases of $U_1, \ldots, U_n$ gives a basis of $V$; so $\dim V = \dim U_1 + \cdots + \dim U_n$.
2. If $V_1, \ldots, V_n$ are finite-dimensional, then $\dim(V_1 \times \cdots \times V_n) = \dim V_1 + \cdots + \dim V_n$.
:::

:::proof
(a) Let $u_{i,1}, \ldots, u_{i,d_i}$ be a basis of $U_i$. Every $v \in V$ is a sum $u_1 + \cdots + u_n$ with $u_i \in U_i$, and each $u_i$ is a combination of $u_{i,1}, \ldots, u_{i,d_i}$; so the combined list spans $V$. If $\sum_{i,j} a_{ij} u_{i,j} = 0$, set $x_i = \sum_j a_{ij} u_{i,j} \in U_i$. Then $x_1 + \cdots + x_n = 0$, so every $x_i = 0$ by independence of the $U_i$, and then every $a_{ij} = 0$ by independence of the basis of $U_i$.

(b) The product $V_1 \times \cdots \times V_n$ is the internal direct sum of the subspaces $\{0\} \times \cdots \times V_i \times \cdots \times \{0\}$, each isomorphic to $V_i$ and hence of dimension $\dim V_i$ (Corollary [4.7.9](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#corollary-4-7-9)). Apply (a). Explicitly, if $v_{i,1}, \ldots, v_{i,d_i}$ is a basis of $V_i$, then the vectors $(0, \ldots, 0, v_{i,j}, 0, \ldots, 0)$, with $v_{i,j}$ in position $i$, form a basis of $V_1 \times \cdots \times V_n$.
:::

:::example{4.7.15}
**Dimensions:**

- $\dim k^n = n$: the standard basis has $n$ elements.
- $\dim k[x]_{\leq d} = d + 1$: the monomials $1, x, \ldots, x^d$ form a basis.
- $k[x]$ is infinite-dimensional: any finite list of polynomials has bounded degree, so its span contains no polynomial of larger degree.
- $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ and $k^\infty$ are infinite-dimensional, since they contain the infinite-dimensional subspace $k[x]$, respectively the eventually zero sequences (Proposition [4.7.10](/notes/math-55a/4-7-finite-dimensional-vector-spaces-and-dimension#proposition-4-7-10)).
:::

:::question{4.7.16}
<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. Show that the monomials $1, x, x^2, \ldots$ are linearly independent in $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ but do not span it.
2. Suppose $V$ has a countable spanning set. Show that every linearly independent subset of $V$ is countable.
3. Show that $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ contains an uncountable linearly independent subset. Conclude that $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ has no countable spanning set, and in particular no countable basis.

:::solution
**(a)** A linear combination of finitely many distinct monomials is a polynomial, which is $0$ only if all its coefficients are $0$; so the monomials are independent. For the same reason their span is $k[x]$, and a power series such as $\sum_{i=0}^\infty x^i$, with infinitely many nonzero coefficients, is not in it.

**(b)** Let $s_0, s_1, s_2, \ldots$ span $V$ (a finite spanning set can be padded with zeros) and put $V_n = \Span(s_0, \ldots, s_n)$. Every vector is a finite linear combination of the $s_i$, so $V = \bigcup_n V_n$. Let $I \subseteq V$ be linearly independent. Any distinct elements of $I \cap V_n$ form an independent list in a space spanned by $n + 1$ vectors, so by the exchange lemma $I \cap V_n$ has at most $n + 1$ elements. Hence $I = \bigcup_n (I \cap V_n)$ is a countable union of finite sets, and it is countable: list the elements of $I \cap V_0$, then the new elements of $I \cap V_1$, and so on.

**(c)** Let $T$ be the set of finite strings of $0$’s and $1$’s, including the empty string. It is countable, since there are $2^l$ strings of each length $l$; fix a bijection $\beta : T \to \NN$. For an infinite $0$–$1$ sequence $t = (t_1, t_2, \ldots)$, let $$A_t = \{\beta(t_1 t_2 \cdots t_l) : l \geq 0\} \subseteq \NN$$ be the set of codes of the initial segments of $t$, and let $f_t = \sum_{n \in A_t} x^n \in k\llbracket x \rrbracket$. Each $A_t$ is infinite, since initial segments of different lengths are different strings. If $t \neq t'$ and the two sequences first differ at position $l_0$, their common initial segments are those of length less than $l_0$, so $A_t \cap A_{t'}$ is finite. In particular $f_t \neq f_{t'}$.

The $f_t$ are linearly independent. Suppose $\sum_{i=1}^m c_i f_{t_i} = 0$ with distinct $t_1, \ldots, t_m$. The set $A_{t_1} \setminus (A_{t_2} \cup \cdots \cup A_{t_m})$ is infinite, since it is obtained from the infinite set $A_{t_1}$ by removing the finite sets $A_{t_1} \cap A_{t_i}$; for $n$ in it, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $\sum c_i f_{t_i}$ is $c_1$. So $c_1 = 0$, and likewise every $c_i = 0$.

An infinite $0$–$1$ sequence is a function $S \to \{0, 1\}$ on the countably infinite set $S = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, and $|\{0,1\}^S| = |\mcP(S)| > |S|$ by Cantor’s theorem (Theorem [1.7.7](/notes/math-55a/1-7-cardinality#theorem-1-7-7) and the discussion after it). So the set of infinite $0$–$1$ sequences is uncountable, and since $t \mapsto f_t$ is injective, $\{f_t\}$ is an uncountable linearly independent subset of $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$. By (b), $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ has no countable spanning set.

That $k\llbracket x \rrbracket$ has a basis at all follows from the theorem that every vector space has a basis, a consequence of Zorn’s lemma that we do not prove. The proof of that theorem gives no way of writing a basis down.
:::
:::
